mainTopic: Why the רבנן forbid כהנים wine nowadays but not long hair; the 'day before' rule for days in מגילת תענית
overview: The גמרא finishes אביי's point that כהנים drink wine nowadays only according to רבי, which means the רבנן forbid it. So why do the רבנן not also forbid כהנים to grow long hair nowadays? The first answer is that if the בית המקדש is suddenly rebuilt, a כהן can cut his hair at once, but wine takes time to wear off. A nap does not reliably help, because it only sobers someone who drank a רביעית. רב אשי gives a different answer: wine invalidates the עבודה and long hair does not. The גמרא tests this against a ברייתא that gives long hair the death penalty, learned from neighboring פסוקים in יחזקאל. It concludes that this was an old oral tradition, which יחזקאל attached to a פסוק, and that the tradition covers only the death penalty. The גמרא then turns to the משנה's rule that a day listed in מגילת תענית also forbids eulogizing on the day before. It explains why ראש חודש ניסן is included: Torah holidays need no reinforcement, but rabbinic days do. Finally, רב פפא begins to explain why the list runs until the end of פסח, and his answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: כהנים drink wine nowadays following רבי
steps.stepSummary: אביי's answer: כהנים today drink wine following רבי, who permits it now that the בית המקדש is destroyed.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is in accordance with רבי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes אביי's statement from the previous amud. Whose view lets כהנים drink wine nowadays? The view of רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the previous amud, רבי said he would ideally forbid כהנים to drink wine forever, but in practice he permits it (שתקנתו קלקלתו). So the common practice of כהנים drinking wine today follows רבי alone.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי יהודה הנשיא, the editor of the משנה

phrases.english: It is in accordance with Rabbi.
phrases.notes: Completes אביי's answer to 'כמאן שתו כהני האידנא חמרא' on the previous amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes אביי's answer, begun on the previous amud, to the question of whose view כהנים follow when they drink wine nowadays.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: כהנים nowadays drink wine following רבי, who permits it in practice.

steps.title: So the רבנן must forbid long hair too
steps.stepSummary: If רבי permits, then the רבנן forbid, so they should forbid long hair nowadays as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: This implies that the רבנן forbid it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference that causes a problem. If only רבי permits wine nowadays, then the רבנן forbid it. So why do they not also forbid כהנים to grow their hair long nowadays?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wine and long hair are parallel bans for a כהן who serves. If the רבנן keep the wine ban in force today, the long-hair ban should also apply today. Since it does not, the גמרא must explain the difference, which step 3 does.

keyTerms.meaning: By implication / from the fact that

phrases.english: By implication, the Rabbis forbid it!
phrases.notes: An inference that raises a problem: should the רבנן also forbid long hair nowadays?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a problematic implication from the identification in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The practice that כהנים today may grow long hair, even though the רבנן forbid them wine today.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רבנן forbid wine nowadays. If long hair is like wine, they should forbid long hair nowadays too.

steps.title: Hair can be cut quickly, but wine takes time
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן forbid wine in case the בית המקדש is suddenly rebuilt. Long hair is not a problem, because it can be cut right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Perhaps the בית המקדש will be rebuilt soon, and we will need a כהן fit for the עבודה, and there will be none. Here, with hair, he can cut it and go in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the רבנן forbid wine but not long hair. The reason for the wine rule does not apply to hair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that the בית המקדש might be rebuilt suddenly and no כהן would be ready to serve. A כהן who drank wine needs time to sober up. A כהן with long hair can get a haircut and serve right away, so there is no need for a גזירה about hair.

keyTerms.meaning: The בית המקדש may be rebuilt speedily

steps.whyThisMatters: This answer explains the purpose of the רבנן's גזירה. It is a practical worry about readiness, not a ban on wine for its own sake.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: Introduces the reason the רבנן forbid wine.

phrases.english: The Temple may be rebuilt speedily,
and we will need a priest fit for the service
and there will be none.
phrases.notes: This is because they all drank wine.

phrases.english: Here, it is possible for him to cut his hair and enter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem raised in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the two cases by the reason behind the גזירה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Wine and long hair are one category, so the רבנן should forbid both nowadays.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wine rule exists because sobering up takes time. Hair can be fixed instantly, so the רבנן made no rule about it.

steps.title: Sleep also sobers a person quickly
steps.stepSummary: If quick fixes remove the need for a rule, then wine should be allowed too, since רמי בר אבא says a little sleep sobers a person.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, a person who drank wine can also sleep a little and go in, like רמי בר אבא. For רמי בר אבא said: walking a מיל, or a tiny amount of sleep, removes the effect of wine!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of step 3. Wine also seems to have a quick fix, so it should not need a rule either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 3 said hair is allowed because it can be fixed fast. רמי בר אבא teaches that even a small nap gets rid of the wine's effect. If so, the wine case also has a fast fix, and the difference between wine and hair falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: Walking the distance of a מיל

phrases.english: If so, one who drank wine too —
it is possible for him to sleep a little and enter,
in accordance with Rami bar Abba.
For Rami bar Abba said:
Walking a mil, and sleep of any amount —
dispel the wine!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction made in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that wine, unlike hair, cannot be fixed quickly.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רמי בר אבא says a tiny nap sobers a person. So wine can also be fixed quickly, and by the logic of step 3 there should be no גזירה on wine either.

steps.title: A nap helps only after a small amount of wine
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר אבא's rule only applies to someone who drank a רביעית. More than that, walking tires him and sleep makes him more drunk.
steps.simpleTranslation: Wasn't it said about this, that רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: they taught this only when he drank a רביעית. But if he drank more than a רביעית, walking wears him out all the more, and sleep makes him more drunk.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the answer of step 3 by limiting רמי בר אבא's rule. A nap does not always sober a person, so wine still has no guaranteed quick fix.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sleep or walking only helps after a small amount, a רביעית. A כהן who drank more would get more tired from walking and more drunk from sleeping. Since we cannot be sure a quick fix exists for wine, the רבנן's גזירה still makes sense, and the difference from hair stands.

keyTerms.meaning: They taught this only in the case of
A quarter-לוג, a set measure of liquid

steps.confusionAlert: This step does not reject רמי בר אבא. It accepts his rule but limits it to a רביעית of wine.

phrases.english: Wasn't it stated about it,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said that Rabba bar Avuh said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּשֶׁשָּׁתָה שִׁיעוּר רְבִיעִית,
phrases.english: They taught this only when he drank the measure of a quarter-log,
but if he drank more than a quarter-log —
all the more so, the walking wears him out
and the sleep makes him drunk.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4 and saves the answer of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the cited source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any nap sobers any drinker, so wine is as easy to fix as hair.
steps.terutzMaskana: A nap only works after a רביעית. Beyond that it makes things worse, so wine still needs a גזירה.
steps.whatToRemember: First approach: the רבנן forbid wine nowadays because sobering up is not guaranteed to be fast. Long hair can always be cut immediately, so they did not forbid it.

steps.title: רב אשי: wine ruins the עבודה, long hair does not
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a different reason. The רבנן made a גזירה about wine because it makes the עבודה invalid, while long hair does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: those who drank wine make the עבודה invalid, so the רבנן made a גזירה about them. Those with long hair do not make the עבודה invalid, so the רבנן did not make a גזירה about them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers a new and separate way to explain why wine is forbidden nowadays but long hair is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of asking how fast each problem can be fixed, רב אשי looks at how serious each one is. A כהן who drank wine makes his עבודה invalid, so the רבנן protected against it with a גזירה. Long hair, he holds, does not invalidate the עבודה, so no גזירה was needed.

keyTerms.meaning: A late אמורא, a main editor of the בבלי
Who desecrate, meaning invalidate, the עבודה
They decreed / made a rabbinic safeguard

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Those who drank wine, who desecrate the service —
the Rabbis decreed about them.
Those with long hair, who do not desecrate the service —
the Rabbis did not decree about them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, independent answer to the problem of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases by how severe each one is
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Wine and long hair have the same status, so both should be forbidden nowadays.
steps.terutzMaskana: Wine invalidates the עבודה and long hair does not, so only wine received a גזירה.

steps.title: A ברייתא: long hair is punished by death like wine
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists both drunk כהנים and long-haired כהנים among those punished by death, which challenges רב אשי.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: these are the ones punished by death: those who drank wine, and those with long hair.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge רב אשי. Long hair appears to be as serious as wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא puts long hair right next to wine as a sin punished by מיתה בידי שמים. That suggests long hair is equally serious and, like wine, should invalidate the עבודה. This weakens רב אשי's claim that long hair does not invalidate the עבודה.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection from a ברייתא
Punished by death, meaning מיתה בידי שמים

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
And these are the ones who are liable to death:
those who drank wine, and those with long hair.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's answer from step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's claim that long hair does not invalidate the עבודה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא treats long hair like wine, as a death-penalty sin. That suggests long hair is just as serious and should also invalidate the עבודה.

steps.title: Where do we learn the death penalty for long hair?
steps.stepSummary: The death penalty for wine is written clearly in the פסוק. The גמרא asks for the source of the death penalty for long hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for those who drank wine, since it is written clearly about them: 'Do not drink wine or strong drink.' But for those with long hair, where do we learn it from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask for the source of the ברייתא's ruling about long hair. This sets up the next step, which will bring a derivation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For wine, the Torah clearly links drinking and death in ויקרא י:ט. For long hair, no פסוק openly says the punishment is death. The answer to this question will matter for judging whether רב אשי's position holds up.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not drink wine or strong drink (ויקרא י:ט)
From where do we know it?

phrases.english: Granted, those who drank wine —
it is explicitly written about them:
"Drink no wine nor strong drink"
phrases.notes: ויקרא י:ט. The verse ends 'that you should not die.'

phrases.english: But those with long hair, from where do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the long-hair ruling in the ברייתא cited in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for the death penalty of a כהן who serves with long hair.

steps.title: Long hair is linked to wine in the פסוקים, so both carry the death penalty
steps.stepSummary: In יחזקאל, the ban on long hair comes right before the ban on wine. This closeness (a היקש) teaches that long hair is punished by death, just like wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'They shall not shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long,' and right after it is written: 'No כהן shall drink wine when they enter the inner courtyard.' Long-haired כהנים are linked to כהנים who drank wine. Just as those who drank wine are punished by death, long-haired כהנים are also punished by death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 8: where do we learn the death penalty for long hair? It points to two פסוקים in יחזקאל that sit right next to each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah clearly gives death for a כהן who serves after drinking wine. יחזקאל places the long-hair rule right before the wine rule. Because they sit together, they are linked (a היקש), so long hair also gets the death penalty.

keyTerms.meaning: They were linked together (by a היקש, a comparison from nearby verses)

phrases.english: As it is written: 'They shall not shave their heads,'
'nor let their hair grow long,'
and it is written right after it:
'No priest shall drink wine'
'when they enter the inner courtyard,'
so long-haired priests are linked to priests who drank wine:
just as those who drank wine are punished by death,
so too long-haired priests are punished by death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A היקש from the side-by-side פסוקים in יחזקאל 44:20-21 gives long hair the same death penalty as wine.

steps.title: If they are linked, long hair should also make the עבודה invalid
steps.stepSummary: If long hair is compared to wine, the comparison should go all the way. Wine makes the עבודה invalid, so long hair should too, and that would break רב אשי's distinction.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from this same link we could say: just as those who drank wine make the עבודה invalid, long-haired כהנים should also make the עבודה invalid!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the link it just made. If long hair is compared to wine, it should also share wine's other law, making the עבודה invalid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי (step 6) said wine got a גזירה because it invalidates the עבודה, and long hair does not. A full comparison would give long hair that same power too, and then רב אשי's reason would fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: And from it (from this very source)
Who make the Temple service invalid (desecrate it)

phrases.english: And from it:

phrases.aramaic: אִי מָה שְׁתוּיֵי יַיִן דְּמַחֲלִי עֲבוֹדָה —
phrases.english: if just as those who drank wine invalidate the service,
so too long-haired priests should invalidate the service!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how far the היקש of step 9 reaches
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's distinction (step 6), using the היקש of step 9
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A היקש normally compares the two cases fully, so long hair should also invalidate the עבודה, like wine.

steps.title: The link is only for the death penalty
steps.stepSummary: The link between long hair and wine was made only about the death penalty. It was never made about invalidating the עבודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. When they were linked, they were linked only for the death penalty. For invalidating the עבודה, they were not linked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by limiting the comparison. Long hair and wine are compared only for the death penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The link has a limited job: it teaches death and nothing more. So long hair does not invalidate the עבודה, and רב אשי's distinction stays in place.

phrases.english: No:
when they were linked, it was only for death that they were linked,
but for invalidating the service, they were not linked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the היקש
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The היקש makes long hair equal to wine in every way, including invalidating the עבודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The היקש covers only the death penalty, so long hair does not invalidate the עבודה.

steps.title: Who taught this law before יחזקאל?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks: if the long-hair law comes from יחזקאל, who taught it before he lived? A נביא cannot create new laws.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: Before יחזקאל came, who said this law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges the source from step 9. The law seems to come from a later נביא, so how did anyone know it before him?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נביא may not add new laws to the Torah. If the long-hair law first appears in יחזקאל, it seems either it did not exist before him or he invented it, and both are a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא, a colleague and student of רב אשי

steps.confusionAlert: רבינא is not denying the law. He is asking where it came from before יחזקאל, because a נביא cannot make up new הלכה.

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
This law, before Yechezkel came,
who said it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the source used in step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: Deriving the long-hair law from יחזקאל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A נביא cannot make new laws, so the law must have existed before יחזקאל. Where did it come from?

steps.title: Your question also hits רב חסדא's law about an uncircumcised כהן
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי turns the question around. רב חסדא says the ban on an uncircumcised כהן serving also comes only from יחזקאל, so the same question applies there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to him: By your reasoning, take what רב חסדא said: 'We did not learn this from the Torah of משה, we learned it from דברי קבלה: No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart or uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter My מקדש.' Before יחזקאל came, who said that?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי does not answer yet. He shows that רבינא's question would also hit an accepted law, which sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone accepts that an uncircumcised כהן may not serve, and רב חסדא says its source is יחזקאל. So the question is not special to long hair, and both cases need the same explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: And according to your reasoning (turning the question back)
Words of tradition, meaning נביאים and כתובים

phrases.english: He said to him: And according to your reasoning,
that which Rav Chisda said:

phrases.aramaic: דָּבָר זֶה מִתּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה לֹא לָמַדְנוּ,
phrases.english: 'This matter we did not learn from the Torah of Moshe,'
'but we learned it from the words of tradition:'
'No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart'

phrases.aramaic: וְעֶרֶל בָּשָׂר לֹא יָבוֹא אֶל מִקְדָּשִׁי״ —
phrases.english: 'or uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter My Sanctuary,'
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 44:9; refers to an uncircumcised כהן serving

phrases.english: this law, before Yechezkel came,
who said it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns רבינא's question back on him with a parallel case
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Shows the question cannot be a reason to reject the long-hair source, since it applies just as much to an accepted law
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The question proves too much: it would also cancel רב חסדא's law about an uncircumcised כהן.

steps.title: It was an oral tradition, and יחזקאל attached it to a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The law was known all along as an oral tradition. יחזקאל did not invent it. He only connected it to a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it was learned as a tradition, and יחזקאל came and attached it to a פסוק.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives the real answer to the question about רב חסדא's law: it was always known as an oral tradition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יחזקאל did not create a new law, which a נביא cannot do. He wrote a known oral law into a פסוק as support, called an אסמכתא.

keyTerms.meaning: It was learned as a received oral tradition
He attached (supported) it on a verse

phrases.english: Rather, it was learned as a tradition,
and Yechezkel came and attached it to a verse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the parallel question raised in step 13
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the role of the פסוק: tradition first, פסוק as support
steps.terutzHavaAmina: יחזקאל is the original source of the law.
steps.terutzMaskana: The law is an old oral tradition, and יחזקאל only attached it to a פסוק.

steps.title: The long-hair tradition covers only the death penalty
steps.stepSummary: The same is true for long hair: it was an oral tradition that יחזקאל attached to a פסוק. That tradition taught only the death penalty, not that the עבודה is invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it was learned as a tradition, and יחזקאל came and attached it to a פסוק. When they learned the הלכה, it was for death. For invalidating the עבודה, they did not learn it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי applies the same answer to long hair and finishes the topic. The tradition said only death, which supports his distinction from step 6.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the law comes from a tradition, its reach depends on what the tradition said. It said death and not invalid עבודה. So wine (which invalidates) needed a גזירה, and long hair did not.

keyTerms.meaning: A law (here, a received oral law)

steps.whatToRemember: A long-haired כהן is punished by death, based on an oral tradition that יחזקאל attached to a פסוק. But he does not make the עבודה invalid, unlike a כהן who drank wine. That is why רב אשי says the רבנן made a גזירה on wine and not on hair.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a key idea: some laws in נביאים are really old oral traditions given a פסוק for support, and how far they reach depends on the tradition, not on the פסוק.

phrases.english: Here too: it was learned as a tradition,
and Yechezkel came and attached it to a verse,
and when they learned the law, it was for death;
for invalidating the service, they did not learn it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the answer of step 14 to long hair and answers רבינא (step 12)
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The long-hair law is an old oral tradition that יחזקאל attached to a פסוק. It brings death but does not invalidate the עבודה, so רב אשי's distinction holds.

steps.title: The משנה's rule: the day before is also forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה. If מגילת תענית says not to eulogize on a day, eulogizing is also forbidden on the day before, but allowed on the day after.
steps.simpleTranslation: Any day about which מגילת תענית writes 'not to eulogize': on the day before it, eulogizing is forbidden; on the day after it, eulogizing is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה about the special days in מגילת תענית. This sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מגילת תענית is an ancient list of happy days that celebrate miracles and victories. On some of those days fasting and eulogizing were banned. The משנה adds a 'buffer': the ban also covers the day before, but not the day after.

keyTerms.meaning: An ancient list of festive days on which fasting (and sometimes eulogizing) is forbidden

phrases.english: Any day about which it is written in Megillat Taanit
"not to eulogize"
the day before it is forbidden,
the day after it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of the כהן with long hair is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On a 'no eulogizing' day in מגילת תענית, eulogizing is forbidden the day before and permitted the day after.

steps.title: The opening lines of מגילת תענית
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes the start of מגילת תענית. From ראש חודש ניסן to the 8th (for the תמיד offering), and from the 8th to the end of פסח (for שבועות), eulogizing is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: These are the days on which one may not fast, and on some of them one may not eulogize either. From ראש חודש ניסן until the 8th of the month, the תמיד offering was set up properly, so one may not eulogize on them. From the 8th of the month until the end of the holiday (פסח), the holiday of שבועות was restored, so one may not eulogize on them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the actual text of מגילת תענית that the משנה was talking about. This sets up the question the גמרא will ask next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two celebrations are listed. The first runs from ראש חודש ניסן to the 8th and marks a victory about how the תמיד offering was funded. The second runs from the 8th to the end of פסח and marks a victory about the correct date of שבועות. The key detail to notice is that the first period begins on ראש חודש itself.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Rabbis taught.' This introduces a ברייתא.
The beginning of the month (ראש חודש)
The תמיד, the daily communal offering

steps.confusionAlert: Fasting and eulogizing are two separate bans. All the days on the list ban fasting. Only some of them also ban eulogizing.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
These are the days on which not to fast,
and on some of them not to eulogize:
From the beginning of the month of Nisan
until the eighth of it,
the daily offering was established,
so as not to eulogize on them.
From the eighth of it until the end of the festival,
the festival of Shavuot was restored,
so as not to eulogize on them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אִלֵּין יוֹמַיָּא דְּלָא לְהִתְעַנָּאָה בְּהוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the actual text of the list that the משנה refers to.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eulogizing is banned from ראש חודש ניסן through the 8th, and from the 8th through the end of פסח.

steps.title: Why list ראש חודש if it is already a holiday?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why מגילת תענית starts its list from ראש חודש ניסן. ראש חודש is already a holiday on which eulogizing is forbidden, so the list could have started from the 2nd of ניסן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'From ראש חודש ניסן until the 8th, the תמיד was established, so do not eulogize.' Why do I need it to say 'from ראש חודש'? Let it say 'from the 2nd of ניסן,' since ראש חודש itself is a holiday and eulogizing is already forbidden then!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא re-quotes the first line of the list and challenges its wording. Why include a day that is already forbidden anyway?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The assumption is that the list never wastes words. Since ראש חודש already bans eulogizing on its own, adding it to the list seems pointless. So there must be some extra reason it was included.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Master said.' This re-quotes a source the גמרא just brought.
'Why do I need…?' This asks why a word or detail is necessary.

phrases.english: The Master said:

phrases.aramaic: מֵרֵישׁ יַרְחָא דְנִיסָן עַד תְּמָנְיָא בֵּיהּ
phrases.english: From the beginning of Nisan until the eighth of it
the daily offering was established, not to eulogize.
Why do I need 'from the beginning of the month'?
Let it say 'from the second of Nisan,'

phrases.aramaic: וְרֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ גּוּפֵיהּ יוֹם טוֹב הוּא וְאָסוּר!
phrases.english: since Rosh Chodesh itself is a holiday and is forbidden!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the source just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The words 'from ראש חודש ניסן' in מגילת תענית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ראש חודש already bans eulogizing on its own, so listing it again looks unnecessary.

steps.title: רב: listing ראש חודש bans the day before it
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that ראש חודש was listed so that the day before it (the last day of אדר) would also be forbidden, following the rule of the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: It was needed only to forbid the day before it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב explains the purpose of mentioning ראש חודש in the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every day in מגילת תענית also forbids the day before it. Once ראש חודש ניסן is on the list, the day before it becomes forbidden too. Without the listing, that day would not be included.

phrases.english: Rav said:
It was needed only
to forbid the day before it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of why ראש חודש is listed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the listing a new purpose: it extends the ban to the day before.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Listing ראש חודש seemed to add nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Listing it makes the day before ראש חודש ניסן forbidden as well.

steps.title: Isn't the day before ראש חודש already forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back. The day before ראש חודש should already be forbidden simply because it is the day before ראש חודש, a holiday.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the day before it too: you could already get that from the fact that it is the day before ראש חודש!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's answer, saying his extra day is also already covered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every holiday forbids the day before it, then ראש חודש on its own should already forbid the day before. In that case listing it in מגילת תענית still adds nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Derive it from…' This means you already have the law from another source.

phrases.english: And the day before it as well,
derive it

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ יוֹם שֶׁלִּפְנֵי רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ!
phrases.english: from the fact that it is the day before Rosh Chodesh!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that the listing is needed to forbid the day before
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It assumes ראש חודש by itself already forbids the day before, so the listing is still unnecessary.

steps.title: Torah holidays need no extra protective day
steps.stepSummary: ראש חודש is a Torah holiday, and Torah laws do not need a protective 'fence' day before them. So the day before ראש חודש is not forbidden on its own. Only the listing in מגילת תענית makes it forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: ראש חודש is from the Torah, and a Torah law does not need reinforcement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב by explaining that the 'day before' rule does not apply to Torah holidays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra day before a festive day is a 'reinforcement' (חיזוק) so that people take the day seriously. Torah laws are taken seriously anyway, so they get no extra day. That is why רב's point stands: only מגילת תענית's listing forbids the day before ראש חודש ניסן.

phrases.english: Rosh Chodesh is from the Torah,
and a Torah law does not need reinforcement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge and saves רב's explanation.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Draws a distinction between Torah law and rabbinic law.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every holiday, including ראש חודש, automatically forbids the day before it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only rabbinic days need a protective day before them. ראש חודש, a Torah holiday, does not.

steps.title: A ברייתא proves: rabbinic days need reinforcement, Torah days do not
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that days in מגילת תענית forbid fasting before and after them, while שבת and יום טוב forbid only the day itself. The reason: Torah laws need no reinforcement, but rabbinic laws do.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: The days written in מגילת תענית are forbidden before them and after them. שבתות and ימים טובים are themselves forbidden, but the days before and after them are permitted. What is the difference between them? These (שבת and יום טוב) are Torah law, and Torah law needs no reinforcement. These (מגילת תענית days) are rabbinic law, and rabbinic law needs reinforcement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that clearly supports the rule it just used: Torah law needs no reinforcement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא openly states the distinction. Rabbinic festive days get buffer days so people will not treat them lightly. Torah holidays like שבת and יום טוב get no buffer. This confirms why ראש חודש by itself does not forbid the day before it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'As it was taught in a ברייתא.' This introduces a supporting source.
Rabbinic law (the words of the Scribes)

steps.whatToRemember: Rabbinic festive days (מגילת תענית) need a protective day around them. Torah holidays (שבת, יום טוב, ראש חודש) do not. That is why listing ראש חודש ניסן in מגילת תענית adds the ban on the day before it.
steps.confusionAlert: This ברייתא says both the day before and the day after are forbidden, but our משנה said only the day before. Don't let that throw you. The point brought here is only the Torah-vs-rabbinic distinction.
steps.whyThisMatters: The principle that rabbinic laws need extra 'fences' while Torah laws do not explains why rabbinic enactments often come with added protective measures.

phrases.english: As it was taught:
These days that are written in Megillat Taanit,
before them and after them are forbidden;
Shabbatot and festivals,
they themselves are forbidden,
before them and after them are permitted.
And what is the difference between this and that?
These are Torah law,
and Torah law does not need reinforcement;
these are rabbinic law,
and rabbinic law needs reinforcement.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: הַיָּמִים הָאֵלֶּה הַכְּתוּבִין בִּמְגִילַּת תַּעֲנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in step 21 with an explicit ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The principle that Torah law needs no reinforcement, while rabbinic law does
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא contrasting מגילת תענית days with שבת and יום טוב

steps.title: Quoting the line about the 8th of ניסן through the end of the festival
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a line from מגילת תענית: from the 8th of ניסן until the end of פסח, eulogizing is forbidden, because the proper date of שבועות was restored.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: From the 8th of ניסן until the end of the festival of פסח, the festival of שבועות was re-established, so one may not eulogize.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from מגילת תענית. This sets up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line covers the days from the 8th of ניסן through the end of פסח (the 21st). It marks the days on which the correct timing of שבועות was established, so eulogizing on them is forbidden. Notice that the list runs right through the days of פסח itself. That detail is what the גמרא will question next.

keyTerms.meaning: "The Master said". It introduces a quote from an earlier source, here מגילת תענית.
The festival of שבועות (the Festival of Weeks).

phrases.english: The Master said:
From the eighth of it (Nisan) until the end of the festival
the festival of Shavuot was re-established,
phrases.notes: The correct way of setting the date of שבועות won out.

phrases.english: [so that] one may not eulogize.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: מִתְּמָנְיָא בֵּיהּ עַד סוֹף מוֹעֲדָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ראש חודש ניסן line to a new line in מגילת תענית that raises a similar issue.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From the 8th of ניסן through the end of פסח, eulogizing is forbidden.

steps.title: Why include the festival days, which are already forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the list says "until the end of the festival". It could have said "until the festival", since פסח is already a יום טוב on which eulogizing is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need it to say "until the end of the festival"? Let it say "until the festival". The festival itself is a יום טוב, so eulogizing on it is already forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of מגילת תענית. Why list the days of פסח if they are already forbidden anyway?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of question as in Step 18 about ראש חודש. The days of פסח are a Torah holiday, so eulogizing on them is forbidden even without מגילת תענית. The list should have stopped at the start of פסח. Including those days seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: "Why do I need...?" Asks why something is written when it seems unnecessary.
"Let it say". It suggests a shorter wording.

phrases.english: Why do I need "until the end of the festival"?
Let it say "until the festival"!
phrases.notes: In other words, stop the list right before פסח begins.

phrases.aramaic: וּמוֹעֵד גּוּפֵיהּ יוֹם טוֹב הוּא וְאָסוּר!
phrases.english: And the festival itself is a holiday, and [eulogizing] is forbidden!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמָה לִי עַד סוֹף מוֹעֵד, לֵימָא עַד הַמּוֹעֵד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the line quoted in Step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase "until the end of the festival" in מגילת תענית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The days of פסח are already forbidden as a Torah יום טוב, so listing them adds nothing.

steps.title: רב פפא answers using רב's approach
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא begins to answer: just as רב explained earlier, listing a day that is already forbidden is needed for something else. The rest of his answer comes on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: As רב said, it is needed only...
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא starts his answer by pointing back to the method רב used for ראש חודש ניסן. The sentence finishes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 19, רב explained that ראש חודש was listed so that the day next to it would also become forbidden. A Torah holiday does not create a protective day on its own, while a day listed in מגילת תענית does (Steps 21-22). רב פפא applies the same idea here: the days of פסח are listed for a reason beyond themselves. That reason is spelled out in the continuation.

keyTerms.meaning: "As רב said". It applies an earlier explanation to a new case.
"It is needed only..." It introduces the real reason something was written.

steps.confusionAlert: The answer is not finished here. "לֹא נִצְרְכָא" opens the explanation, and the actual reason appears on the next amud.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
As Rav said: it is needed only...
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כִּדְאָמַר רַב — לֹא נִצְרְכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 24 by reusing רב's approach from Step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Applying an earlier principle to a parallel case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Listing the days of פסח seemed useless, since they are already forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Following רב, the listing serves a further purpose beyond the festival days themselves. The details continue on the next amud.
